title: Tokenomics at scale: Track and cap Amazon Bedrock spend per IAM principal with CUR 2.0 and AWS Budgets
author: Arun Chandapillai
contentSnippet: Generative AI spend is hard to attribute. Before an organization expands AI access, CFOs and CTOs usually want three answers: what do we spend per person or per team, can we cap it, and how much work does it take to get there. In our previous post, Tokenomics at Scale: How Jamf Built Real-Time Spend Enforcement for Amazon Bedrock , we explained a custom enforcement loop built on AWS IAM Identity Center , Amazon Athena over Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs , and AWS Lambda . This approach gives near-real-time control, but it requires code you then own and operate. This post shows how to get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code to write for the common case. The approach relies on three things: IAM principal attribution , which Amazon Bedrock records automatically; AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) 2.0 or AWS Cost Explorer for reporting; and AWS Budgets with budget actions for enforcement. By the end, you will have per-identity cost reporting and an automatic guardrail that restricts Amazon Bedrock access when a threshold is crossed. Solution overview The solution has three parts: attribute, report, and enforce. Attribute. Amazon Bedrock captures the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal identity, the IAM user or role , for every inference request. This happens automatically, with no change to your Amazon Bedrock model inference calls. If several people share one role, you add per-user detail with session tags passed at role assumption time. If each person or application has its own role, principal tags on the role are enough. Report. Activate those tags as cost allocation tags, then read the data either in Cost Explorer for a console-only view, or in a CUR 2.0 data export for detailed line-item analysis and SQL queries. Enforce. Create an AWS Budget scoped to Amazon Bedrock and filtered to one identity or tag value, then attach a budget action that applies a Deny IAM policy when the threshold is crossed. The following sections show each part in more detail, alongside the implementation steps. Prerequisites To deploy this solution, you need: An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock model access enabled. Permissions to tag IAM principal , activate cost allocation tags , create data exports , and create budgets and budget actions. Amazon Bedrock accessed through

summary.tldr:
AWS has released a native framework for managing and capping Amazon Bedrock expenditures per IAM principal, eliminating the need for custom-coded enforcement loops like those previously implemented by Jamf. The solution leverages three core AWS services: Amazon Bedrock’s automatic IAM principal logging, AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) 2.0 for granular line-item analysis, and AWS Budgets for automated enforcement.

The architecture functions through a three-stage process: attribution, reporting, and enforcement. Amazon Bedrock automatically logs the IAM user or role for every inference request; organizations can further refine this by using session tags during role assumption or principal tags on roles. Once these tags are activated as cost allocation tags, administrators can track spend via AWS Cost Explorer or SQL queries in CUR 2.0. Enforcement is achieved by configuring an AWS Budget scoped to specific identities or tag values, which triggers an automated IAM 'Deny' policy once a predefined financial threshold is breached.
takeaways: **Attribution Mechanism:** Amazon Bedrock automatically records the IAM principal for every inference request without requiring modifications to existing model invocation code.
**Granular Identification:** Organizations can distinguish between individual users sharing a single role by utilizing session tags passed during role assumption.
**Reporting Tools:** Cost visibility is provided through AWS Cost Explorer for console-based monitoring or CUR 2.0 data exports for detailed SQL-based analysis.
**Automated Enforcement:** AWS Budgets can be configured with budget actions that automatically apply a 'Deny' IAM policy to a specific principal once a spending limit is exceeded.

title: Google’s latest Search upgrade promises better answers to your most complicated questions
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.”

While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement.

The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , at its default high thinking level.

In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode.

In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question.

Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains.

The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode.

Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can

summary.tldr:
Google has introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a new model optimized for fast execution and agentic workflows, marking what the company describes as its most significant Search upgrade to date. While Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon models remain the primary choice for deep reasoning, Hydrogen is engineered to balance speed and intelligence, specifically targeting multi-step tasks and complex user queries. The model is currently rolling out globally to all Google Search users and is available across Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the Antigravity development platform for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

Technically, Hydrogen delivers performance 2.5 times faster than the previous Gemini 3.8 Flash model. Despite its focus on speed, it reportedly outperforms the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index when set to its default 'high' thinking level. The model features four distinct thinking levels—low, medium, high (default), and a new 'xhigh' tier—all designed to optimize for speed and reduced token output. In Search, Hydrogen enhances the 'fan-out' technique, which decomposes complex, multi-part prompts into subqueries to improve the relevance of search results, visual responses, and comparison tables. It also demonstrates improved robustness against typos and natural language nuances, and currently holds the No. 5 ranking on the Agent Arena benchmark for multi-step tasks like data analysis and codebase navigation.
takeaways: **Performance Metric:** Gemini 4 Hydrogen executes tasks 2.5 times faster than the Gemini 3.8 Flash model.
**Benchmark Ranking:** The model is ranked No. 5 on the Agent Arena benchmark for multi-step tasks including deep research and codebase navigation.
**Thinking Tiers:** Hydrogen introduces four configurable thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new 'xhigh' tier, all optimized for lower token counts.
**Search Integration:** The model improves Search 'fan-out' capabilities, allowing for more precise handling of multi-part queries, visual responses, and comparison tables.
**Availability:** The model is available globally in Search, Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the Antigravity development platform.

title: Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands
author: Lauren Forristal
contentSnippet:
Nectar , an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.

Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.

Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.

Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN . The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.

Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.

Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular.

Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.

“Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from the

summary.tldr:
Nectar, an AI-powered marketing operating system founded by former Meta employees Misbah and Farah Uraizee, has launched a new 'Creator Agent' designed to automate the end-to-end influencer marketing lifecycle. The tool handles creator discovery, personalized outreach, contract management, and campaign performance tracking. By leveraging a database of over 300 million creator profiles, the agent performs contextual video analysis to assess brand fit and safety, moving beyond simple keyword matching to evaluate content tone and platform-specific nuances.

The system integrates directly into brand workflows, drafting messages in a brand's specific voice and managing logistical tasks like product gifting and shipping. A notable feature includes monitoring creator milestones—such as life events—to suggest personalized engagement strategies. The agent is currently available globally for Instagram and TikTok, with plans to integrate via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling interoperability with AI assistants like Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot. This launch follows Nectar's $30 million Series A funding round led by Menlo Ventures and the Anthropic-backed Anthology Fund.
takeaways: **Market Scale:** U.S. spending on creator advertising is projected to reach $44 billion by 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau.
**Technical Capabilities:** The agent utilizes proprietary guardrails to maintain brand tone across different platforms, distinguishing between contexts like X quote posts and TikTok comments.
**Data Scope:** The platform indexes more than 300 million creator profiles, prioritizing both established influencers and emerging creators gaining traction.
**Integration Strategy:** Nectar plans to expose the Creator Agent via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to support third-party AI assistants and custom-built agentic workflows.
**Funding Context:** The company secured $30 million in Series A funding in May 2024, led by Menlo Ventures and the Anthology Fund.

title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
author: Hugging Face Blog
contentSnippet:
LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview . We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

Indirect prompt injections, hidden in user data, are mostly ignored by LLMON models due to explicit instruction/data separation. For some benchmarks, attack success rates drop to nearly zero, whereas regular instruction-tuned models get hijacked with high probability. This is achieved while maintaining general capability relative to Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

Unrelated passages, old chat turns, and tool outputs don’t get pulled into the answer because each instruction is bound to the exact data it applies to.

Instructions, data, and requirements are clearly marked so that their structure and meanings at the application’s code level can be leveraged by t

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced LLMON (LLM Object Notation), an LLM-native markup language designed to replace JSON for structuring LLM context. By utilizing XML-like tags wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters, LLMON explicitly separates instructions, data, and requirements, allowing models to bind specific instructions to data payloads. This structural clarity aims to solve the brittleness of smaller models and mitigate indirect prompt injection attacks by ensuring the model treats data and instructions as distinct, addressable entities rather than a flattened string of text.

To support this, two experimental preview models—granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview—have been released, derived from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints. These models were trained on a re-serialized instruction-tuning corpus where every component is an addressable block. Benchmarks on the OPI, ASB, and StruQ datasets indicate that LLMON models achieve near-zero attack success rates against static indirect prompt injections, outperforming the best frontier models by 47% and the best open-source models by 95% in robustness, all while maintaining general capabilities comparable to standard Granite 4.1 Instruct models.
takeaways: **Architecture:** LLMON uses six reserved special tokens as delimiters to define tags, ensuring structural markers are distinct from content tokens, unlike JSON where structural characters (brackets, quotes) are ambiguous.

**Security Performance:** On the OPI benchmark, LLMON models demonstrated 47% higher robustness against indirect prompt injection than the best-tested frontier model and 95% higher than the best open-source model.

**Model Availability:** Two preview models, granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview, are available, alongside a GitHub repository containing conversion tools for existing JSON pipelines.

**Implementation:** The models integrate with standard chat templates via an 'exec' block, which explicitly defines which instructions to run, which data to use, and where to output the result, without requiring manual changes to existing message lists.

**Training Methodology:** Models were trained from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints using a re-serialized instruction-tuning corpus, ensuring LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than applied as a wrapper.

title: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock
author: Majd Arbash
contentSnippet: Part 1 of this series built the operating model that controls Amazon Bedrock spend: attribution with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal tags and Cost and Usage Report 2.0, observability with model invocation logging, enforcement at three tiers, and a review cadence. That layer answers who spent it, and you can stop them. It can’t tell you whether the spend was well spent. This post answers two questions that Part 1 deliberately left open. First: Why is this workflow expensive? The answer requires thinking in cost per task, not cost per token. Second: Is the agent better than the humans were? The answer requires baselines, controlled experiments, and a scorecard tied to decisions. In this post, you learn a framework for calculating true model cost (including four hidden cost drivers that the pricing page doesn’t show), techniques for reducing cost per task through caching, routing, and output constraints, and a discipline for measuring agent ROI with human baselines, holdout experiments, and a five-dimension scorecard. This post is written for two audiences: the application and platform engineers who own the optimization levers, and the product owners and FinOps partners who need to justify agent spend to leadership. Cost per task, not cost per token Price per token invites quick comparison, but it doesn’t reflect what you actually pay. The published rate reflects the cost of a single token. Your bill reflects the cost of completing a task. A task is one complete unit of work your application asks a model to do: resolve one support email, extract fields from one invoice, or answer one user question. A task runs from the request through to a usable result, however many model calls it takes. The lower-priced model might not be the cheaper one to run. A cheaper model might fragment your text into more tokens, pad responses with filler, misread your tool schema and loop through corrections, or burn thousands of reasoning tokens before answering. None of these costs appear on the Bedrock pricing page . The four hidden cost drivers Four model characteristics determine what that published rate actually costs you on your workload. Tokenizer efficiency A token isn’t a word, and it is not equal across models. Every model family uses a different tokenizer and vocabulary. The same text, code, or JSON payload splits into different token counts. If Model A’

summary.tldr:
This article outlines a framework for evaluating Amazon Bedrock expenditure by shifting focus from per-token pricing to 'cost per task.' The author argues that published model rates are insufficient for ROI analysis because they ignore the operational reality of completing a full unit of work, such as resolving a support ticket or extracting invoice data. The methodology emphasizes that lower-priced models can become more expensive due to inefficient tokenization, verbose output, tool-use failures, or excessive reasoning cycles.

To optimize costs, the author proposes a strategy involving caching, intelligent model routing, and strict output constraints. The framework for measuring agent ROI requires establishing human-performance baselines, conducting controlled holdout experiments, and utilizing a five-dimension scorecard. The piece identifies four 'hidden' cost drivers—tokenizer efficiency, output verbosity, tool-use reliability, and reasoning overhead—that significantly impact the final bill but are not visible on standard AWS pricing pages.
takeaways: **Cost Metric:** Shift from per-token pricing to 'cost per task' to account for the total model calls required to complete a single unit of work.
**Hidden Cost Drivers:** Four primary factors influence actual spend: tokenizer efficiency, output verbosity, tool-use schema adherence, and reasoning token consumption.
**Optimization Levers:** Cost reduction strategies include implementing caching, model routing, and enforcing output constraints to minimize unnecessary token usage.
**ROI Methodology:** Agent performance must be validated against human baselines using controlled holdout experiments and a structured five-dimension scorecard.

title: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM
author: Sitaraman Vijay Krishna
contentSnippet: Developers want AI coding assistants with minimal setup. With a large language model (LLM) gateway and LiteLLM, they can quickly access foundation models (FMs) available on Amazon Bedrock while you gain visibility and usage control. Platform teams need to monitor latency and errors, finance teams need to attribute inference costs to teams and projects, and security teams need consistent access controls. An LLM gateway can help address these needs by providing a centrally managed access point to the models that power coding assistants. In this post, we show how to build a self-service LLM gateway using Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles with LiteLLM running on AWS Fargate to abstract Amazon Bedrock behind an OpenAI-compatible API. With this pattern, developers can access foundation models through a single API with a dedicated key while you gain per-user cost controls and model performance observability. By the end, you will understand the pattern well enough to build your own version from the illustrative snippets and AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs. This post uses Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku models for example purposes. For a list of models and availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . This LLM gateway pattern follows a straightforward request flow from the developer, through the LiteLLM layer, to Amazon Bedrock and the underlying FM. The following diagram illustrates the production topology behind that flow. For simplicity, we don’t cover the addition of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, such as content filtering and grounding, but you would normally include appropriate responsible AI controls before deploying to production. A developer’s OpenAI-compatible client reaches the LLM gateway through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB). It authenticates to LiteLLM on Fargate with a per-user API key. Behind that, the request draws on Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) (PostgreSQL) for virtual-key and spend state. It also interacts with Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache, and AWS Secrets Manager for secrets. LiteLLM then ultimately invokes Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles using a scoped AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) task role. Amazon CloudWatch captures requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) metrics and the

summary.tldr:
This technical guide details the implementation of a self-service LLM gateway using LiteLLM and Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles to provide an OpenAI-compatible API for foundation models. By deploying LiteLLM on AWS Fargate, platform teams can centralize model access, enforce per-user API keys, and implement cost attribution and observability for AI coding assistants. The architecture is designed to abstract underlying model complexity while allowing teams to monitor latency, error rates, and token usage.

The production-ready topology utilizes a request flow starting from an OpenAI-compatible client, passing through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to reach the LiteLLM container. State management for virtual keys and spend tracking is handled by Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL), while Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey serves as a caching layer. Secrets are managed via AWS Secrets Manager, and the system uses scoped AWS IAM task roles to invoke Bedrock models, specifically citing Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku as primary examples. Metrics including requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) are captured via Amazon CloudWatch.
takeaways: **Core Architecture:** Combines LiteLLM on AWS Fargate with Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles to create an OpenAI-compatible API gateway.
**State & Caching:** Utilizes Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL) for tracking virtual keys and spend, and Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey for request caching.
**Observability:** Integrates Amazon CloudWatch to monitor key performance indicators including requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM).
**Security & Access:** Employs per-user API keys for authentication and scoped AWS IAM task roles for secure interaction with Bedrock foundation models.
**Deployment Pattern:** Leverages AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs to automate the infrastructure deployment.

title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
author: Rebecca Bellan
contentSnippet:
The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.

Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models.

Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community.

Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US.

Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next.

Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.

Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China.

The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to W

summary.tldr:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following allegations of an affair with an executive linked to an alleged Chinese espionage operation. The departure creates significant uncertainty regarding Nvidia’s strategic commitment to the open-source AI ecosystem, a cause Huang championed as a counterweight to the closed-model dominance of firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. Nvidia has appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, leaving the future of several high-profile initiatives—including a pending $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face and a $6 billion non-exclusive licensing deal with coding startup Poolside—in question.

Huang’s tenure was defined by his aggressive push for open-weight models, most notably the Nemotron family, which Nvidia developed for agentic and reasoning-heavy workloads. He also served as a primary political advocate for the open-source community, leading a coalition of 25 companies—including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir—in an open letter to the U.S. government opposing strict regulations on open-weight AI. These efforts were designed to diversify Nvidia’s customer base beyond the major hyperscalers, who are increasingly developing proprietary silicon, by fostering a broader ecosystem of developers and nation-states reliant on Nvidia’s hardware.
takeaways: **Leadership Transition:** Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO following Jensen Huang's resignation.
**Pending Acquisitions:** The status of Nvidia’s $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face and a $6 billion licensing deal with Poolside is currently unclear.
**Strategic Advocacy:** Huang led a 25-company coalition, including Microsoft and Meta, to lobby against U.S. government restrictions on open-weight AI models.
**Product Focus:** Under Huang, Nvidia prioritized the Nemotron model family, specifically designed for long-running agentic AI and complex reasoning tasks.
**Market Rationale:** Nvidia’s support for open source was a strategic hedge against the vertical integration of major customers like Google and OpenAI, who are building custom AI chips.

The provided text highlights a significant tension between his recent self-identification as a lifelong Democrat and his documented history of nationalist rhetoric and defense of controversial geopolitical stances.
takeaways: **Military Strategy:** Karp has explicitly stated that Palantir’s role is to make the U.S. armed forces "more lethal" by analyzing data to help locate and neutralize targets.

**Ideological Stance:** Karp has publicly identified Palantir as "the first company to be completely anti-woke" and has criticized elite institutions for fostering what he terms a "pagan religion" of sacrifice.

title: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen
author: Google DeepMind
contentSnippet:

title: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime
author: Madhu Parthasarathy
contentSnippet: AI agents have moved past one-off prompts. They now run multi-step workloads for hours at a time. The length of task that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months ( METR ), and 40 percent of large enterprises are scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago ( McKinsey ). As agents run longer and with more autonomy, the focus shifts from what agents can do to how securely, reliably, and economically they can operate at scale. Agents do more than traditional software: they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce new security and infrastructure demands, making strong isolation essential for production deployments. Every agent session needs a secure, isolated environment. But delivering that isolation at scale introduces a fundamental challenge: balancing performance, cost, and efficiency. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs. On-demand environments reduce wasted capacity but introduce cold-start latency, delaying agent execution. Neither approach scales efficiently without trade-offs. As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex, expensive, and unpredictable. The challenge is evident. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they can’t yet trust and govern their agents ( Deloitte ). Scaling agents shouldn’t mean choosing between security, speed, and cost. The next generation of agent infrastructure must deliver strong isolation with fast startup times, elastic scaling, and usage-based economics. Because as AI agents move into production, secure execution shouldn’t be the bottleneck. It should be the foundation that makes scale possible. The fastest path to production should also be the safest one. The next generation AgentCore runtime We built Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help developers build, connect, and optimize agents securely at scale. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the managed compute layer. It gives developers a fully managed environment to deploy and run agents without building or maintaining infrastructure. Since launching, our customers have been pushing their agents into increasingly comp

summary.tldr:
Amazon has introduced the AgentCore runtime, a managed compute layer within Amazon Bedrock AgentCore designed to address the infrastructure challenges of scaling autonomous AI agents. As enterprise adoption grows—with McKinsey reporting that 40% of large enterprises are now scaling AI agents compared to 27% a year ago—the industry faces a bottleneck in balancing secure, isolated execution with performance and cost efficiency. AgentCore aims to eliminate the need for developers to build and maintain custom sandboxes, providing a managed environment that supports the long-running, multi-step workloads characteristic of modern frontier agents.

The runtime addresses the trade-off between pre-provisioned environments, which incur costs during idle time, and on-demand environments, which suffer from cold-start latency. By providing a managed compute layer, AgentCore enables elastic scaling and usage-based economics, allowing organizations to move beyond the current industry trend where only 15% of organizations have successfully scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems. The platform is positioned as a foundational infrastructure component to ensure that secure execution does not impede the deployment of agents that require code execution, browser navigation, and access to sensitive user data.
takeaways: **Market Adoption:** 40% of large enterprises are currently scaling AI agents, up from 27% in the previous year according to McKinsey data.
**Industry Bottleneck:** Only 15% of organizations have successfully scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, with 70% citing a lack of trust and governance as primary barriers.
**Performance Metric:** According to METR, the length of tasks that frontier agents can complete autonomously doubles approximately every four months.

**Core Value Proposition:** Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a managed compute layer to eliminate the infrastructure overhead of custom sandboxes while balancing security, cold-start latency, and resource costs.

title: The Jensen Huang scandal is hardly over

He’s placed himself indispensably at the center of the AI industry and famously had no succession plan at Nvidia. In fact, he’s the only CEO Nvidia has ever had. L’état c’est moi. summary.tldr:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following a series of reports alleging personal misconduct and systemic failures in the company's export compliance. The departure follows allegations of affairs with subordinates, including Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s VP of Healthcare, and Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed—a firm accused of acting as a front for illegal GPU diversion to China. These personal scandals are reportedly being used as a pretext for an ouster driven by the board, as the company faces mounting scrutiny over its adherence to U.S. export controls on high-end AI chips.

Technical and regulatory concerns center on the diversion of Nvidia hardware to blacklisted Chinese entities. Despite Huang’s public claims that Nvidia has zero percent market share in China and no evidence of chip diversion, reports from Culper Research and The New York Times suggest that over 20% of Nvidia’s FY 2026 compute revenues may be tied to China via intermediaries. Specific entities like Megaspeed and Super Micro have been linked to the movement of billions in hardware to Chinese firms, including Alibaba. Furthermore, allegations have surfaced that Nvidia intervened to halt a 2025 Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed, prompting congressional inquiries and potential future subpoenas from the Senate Banking Committee.

**Megaspeed Scandal:** The firm, identified as a major Southeast Asian buyer, was found to have no active operations at its listed addresses and is linked to Alice Huang, who allegedly promised Nvidia Blackwell chips to the Chinese AI firm DeepSeek.
**Super Micro Involvement:** Co-founders of Super Micro allegedly facilitated the purchase of $2.5 billion in Nvidia chips for Alibaba through a Thailand-based front company, OBON.

**Regulatory Scrutiny:** Nvidia reportedly intervened to stop a 2025 Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed, leading to political fallout for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and potential Senate investigations.

**Corporate Governance:** Jensen Huang, Nvidia's only CEO to date, resigned amid board pressure following reports of multiple affairs and allegations of potential criminal involvement in chip smuggling.

title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025.

“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X.

While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models.

The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress were not returned.

title: AWS Releases AWS Emulator: A Local Copy of 200+ AWS Services Built by AI Agents
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: AWS has released AWS Emulator , a local emulator of the AWS APIs. You run it on a laptop, a dev server or in CI. The AWS CLI and SDKs talk to it instead of AWS. No AWS account is needed, and there is no service fee . The unusual part: autonomous agents wrote and reviewed all of its code . For developers and coding agents, AWS Emulator gives a fast, free test loop against AWS-shaped APIs. TL;DR Size: Built from 438 AWS API models , covering 200+ services . One Rust crate per service. Runs on: Linux x86_64/aarch64 (RPM or Debian), or Docker on macOS/Windows with a 2 GiB memory limit. Source builds need 100 GB of free disk. Performance: Passes 24,243 of 42,857 scored fidelity tests (56.6%) in release v1.0.322 . Best: AWS KMS at 93.9% (291 of 310 tests); Amazon SQS at 89.8%. Worst: AWS CloudFormation at 15.8% (414 of 2,612 tests). What is AWS Emulator? AWS Emulator is a headless local program from AWS that serves an AWS API endpoint. You point the CLI or an SDK at it with environment variables. Your code does not change. Resources live in memory and vanish when it stops. The docs show a DynamoDB example. A CreateTable call with a 2-character name fails with the same ValidationException text AWS returns. How did AI agents build AWS Emulator? The project began with a prompt to Kiro . It returned a passable Amazon SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. AWS then split the work across 3 teams of agents: Test writers derive scenarios from the public Smithy API models and verify each against real AWS. Issue finders replay those tests against the emulator and file failures. Fixers take 1 issue each and submit a patch. Every patch passes a merge gate covering build, code review, security and fidelity. Several security agents run adversarial reviews . Matthew Goldberg reports hundreds of concurrent agents fixing thousands of issues a day. The release pipeline runs on AWS Developer Tools, with CodeCommit as the agents’ repository. title: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent
author: Josh DeMuth
contentSnippet: With a customer-managed knowledge base on Amazon Bedrock , you provision and scale the vector store, tune the embedding model and index settings, and plan capacity for each new data source. The migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps you migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base . Managed Knowledge Base takes over that work and adds new retrieval capabilities, and your team keeps control of the content and the application that uses it. Moving a production knowledge base means your team maps its configuration, creates the replacement, ingests content, updates the application’s retrieval call, and validates retrieval before switching traffic. To help, we added a knowledge base migration guide to the amazon-bedrock skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS . The guide gives your coding agent the context to plan the migration with you, starting with read-only discovery and a plan you review line by line. On your approval, the agent creates the new knowledge base and its data sources alongside the original, or writes a migrated infrastructure as code (IaC) template for your pipeline. Ingestion and updating your application’s Retrieve calls stay with you, and your agent can walk you through both. In this post, we explain why we recommend the move and how the migration guide works, review the prerequisites, install the skill, plan a migration, update the application’s retrieval call, and validate retrieval before cutover. Why move to Managed Knowledge Base We recommend Managed Knowledge Base because it balances ease of use, retrieval accuracy, and cost. AWS runs the store With a Managed Knowledge Base, Amazon Bedrock handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval, and the store scales automatically as your content grows. Hybrid search, which combines keyword and semantic matching, is always on, with no index to configure. The knowledge base includes a managed embedding model, a managed reranker, and a built-in parser for multimodal file types. You can still bring your own Amazon Bedrock embedding model when you create the knowledge base. title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
author: Amit Chaudhary
contentSnippet: Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides. The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use. While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running. In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test. The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project , and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks. In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A , we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. title: Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools
author: Renya Kujirada
contentSnippet: More enterprises are building AI agents into their daily work, and a common pattern is an agent that searches internal documents to compose its answers. A single organization might soon run hundreds of agents, each connected to many data sources and tools. This raises a question. When an agent searches on behalf of a user, can you make sure that it uses only the information that user is allowed to see? Consider AnyCompany, a fictional company that builds an internal assistant shared by all employees. An employee in department A asks, “Compare my department’s business plan with the notice to all departments, and list the initiatives that are behind schedule.” The agent writes its own search queries and keeps searching internal documents until it has enough information. Employees in department B ask the same assistant the same question. If the application doesn’t scope searches to each user, the department B business plan can end up in an answer to an employee in department A. If you replace the departments with customer companies, the same problem occurs in a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) architecture where multiple customers share one assistant and knowledge base. Controlling access to multi-tenant data through this agent is harder than in traditional applications. In a traditional application, the application code determines who the signed-in user is and searches with that user’s permissions. In an agent, a large language model (LLM) decides at runtime which tool to call and with which arguments. If a search tool takes “who to search as” as an argument, the LLM decides that value too. A prompt injection or an LLM error might then make the agent search as a different employee. In this post, we build an internal assistant for AnyCompany. All employees share the same agent and knowledge base, yet each employee can search only the documents they’re allowed to view. We use Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base as the search backend and expose it to the agent as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The design principle is to not let the LLM decide who the user is. Instead, trusted code decides, based on information that your identity provider has verified. title: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC
author: Yuan Wei
contentSnippet: Over the past year, AI agents have moved from exploration into engineering. Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge. A successful demo can show what an agent is capable of. Before release, the team needs to answer a further question: “ Is this agent ready for production? ” The person responsible for that decision needs evidence that the agent meets the agreed requirements. To make that decision consistently, teams need a repeatable, affordable way to assess the agent’s current behavior and whether the latest change has improved it. In traditional software development, teams answer these questions with unit tests, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), and passing builds. Those mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient for agents, for three reasons, each requiring additional checks. This post explains these three properties and presents a measured case where an aggregate metric hides a coverage problem. It then introduces the Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC): one lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change. A note on terminology:  Throughout this post, gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against. Business owners approve this standard as the basis for acceptance decisions. 1. Three properties of agents that require additional engineering practices Conventional software testing and CI/CD still apply to agents, but three properties require additional checks. First, agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths. Second, changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal. Third, model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior. title: Agents that build their own databases are forcing a data foundation rethink
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 06:02 EST / NOVEMBER 12 2026

Agents that build their own databases are forcing a data foundation rethink

AI agents are changing how enterprises create, move and govern information, and data observability is turning into a prerequisite rather than a nice-to-have. Models get most of the attention, but the data beneath them decides whether they hold up in production.

That pressure is now reaching the cloud-native community, where KubeCon organizers added a dedicated AI inference and agentic track this year. The industry has raced from chatbots to retrieval, fine-tuning and agents, yet every wave rests on the same groundwork, according to Sanjeev Mohan (pictured), principal at SanjMo, a data and AI advisory firm, and author of “Designing the AI-Driven Data Foundations.”

“AI can only be successful if it’s built on a solid foundation,” Mohan said. “You have no observability or transparency into it. No matter what you do on top of it, it will not be successful.”

Mohan spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed theCUBE’s second day of coverage at the event. (* Disclosure below.)

Why AI agents demand data observability at runtime

For decades, data was created once in an operational system and then pushed through brittle pipelines for extraction, transformation, cataloging and preparation. That model works when humans consume batch reports, Mohan explained. Thousands of agents change the math.

“They’re not going to wait for this pipeline to finish. They want access to the database directly,” Mohan said.

Agents are also doing something no earlier software did. They spin up short-lived databases, copy data and test different chains of thought before picking one action, according to Mohan. An agent reviewing a loan application might query census records and social media before rejecting it, which raises the question of how that decision gets audited.

“Governance becomes really important, and this is not like governance in the past where you would govern your data and then have a deterministic CFO report dashboard run on it,” Mohan said.

That makes data observability part of the architecture itself, not an afterthought bolted onto a warehouse. Mohan’s book, published in June 2026 by John Wiley & Sons Inc

summary.tldr:
Sanjeev Mohan, principal at SanjMo and author of "Designing the AI-Driven Data Foundations" (published June 2026 by John Wiley & Sons), argues that the rise of autonomous AI agents necessitates a fundamental shift in enterprise data architecture. Traditional data models, which rely on batch processing and brittle extraction-transformation-loading (ETL) pipelines, are insufficient for agents that require direct, real-time database access to perform tasks. Mohan emphasizes that data observability must transition from a post-hoc monitoring tool to a core architectural requirement to ensure transparency and auditability in agentic decision-making.

Agents are increasingly creating short-lived, ephemeral databases to test various "chains of thought" and build context at runtime. This behavior creates a challenge for governance, as agents may query diverse sources—such as census records and social media—to inform a single decision, such as a loan rejection. Mohan posits that future data platforms must evolve into converged systems capable of handling both structured and unstructured data, as the context required for agentic tasks is highly dynamic and unique to each specific execution instance.
takeaways: **Architectural Shift:** AI agents are moving away from batch-processed data pipelines toward direct, runtime database access.
**Ephemeral Databases:** Agents are increasingly spinning up short-lived, temporary databases to test decision paths and store context during execution.
**Governance Challenge:** Traditional deterministic reporting dashboards are inadequate for auditing agentic decisions that rely on dynamic, runtime-generated context.
**Converged Systems:** Future data foundations must integrate structured and unstructured data into a single, observable architecture to support agentic workflows.

title: Nebuly wants to help enterprises understand exactly what their AI investments are worth after raising $21M
author: Mike Wheatley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 05:00 EST / NOVEMBER 12 2026

Nebuly wants to help enterprises understand exactly what their AI investments are worth after raising $21M

An Italian startup called Nebuly S.r.l. says it’s going to help organizations better understand the impact their investments in artificial intelligence have on their bottom lines after raising $21 million in funding today.

The round was led by Planven and saw participation from backers including Exor Ventures, Tenacity Capital, TGVG Capital, Fastweb, Vodafone and CDP Venture Capital’s Digital Transition Fund.

The world’s biggest companies have been spending millions of dollars on artificial intelligence, but very few can actually say how much value those investments have returned. Though some leaders might be able to point to a few vanity metrics, they’ll likely stumble if pressed to come up with concrete numbers.

This is a problem because enterprise leaders are increasingly feeling the pressure to justify their investments in AI. A recent Gartner Inc. survey of business leaders found that 85% of respondents plan to step up their AI spending in the next year, but at the same time, only 22% say they have managed to scale the technology across multiple business units.

Meanwhile, spending is spiraling out of control at many companies. Famously, Uber Technologies Inc. revealed earlier this year that it had eaten up the entire budget it set aside for AI in 2026 in just four months.

Nebuly co-founder and Chief Executive Franceso Signorato told SiliconANGLE that one of the main challenges when it comes to understanding AI’s return on investment is that many companies have deployed a jumbled patchwork of AI models and applications. They’re using tools from OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic PBC, Microsoft Corp., Google LLC and others, as well as developing in-house tools under their own steam.

That makes it harder to see which projects are actually paying off and generating real business revenue. Although companies can track superficial metrics like token consumption and prompt tallies, genuine productivity gains remain obscured.

“Every enterprise is about to face the same question from its board, if it hasn’t already: What is AI actually worth to us? Nebuly exists to answer that question,” Signorato said. “Until now companies have measured AI by counting users, prompts and responses, which has fueled the rise of tokenmaxx

title: IBM Announces IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3: A New Processor to Support 10k Quantum Operations on 520 Programmable Qubits
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: IBM has announced IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3 , its next superconducting quantum processor. It is designed to run 10,000 quantum operations accurately across 520 programmable qubits. In 2027, IBM plans to link 2 r3 chips into a single 1,040-qubit system. For developers, the announcement is speed. The current Nighthawk r2 already runs workloads up to 19x faster than IBM’s earlier processors. TL;DR Size: Nighthawk r3: 520 programmable qubits, 2,034 physical qubits, 10 l-couplers. Nighthawk r2 (live today): 120 programmable qubits, 218 couplers. Runs on: IBM Quantum Platform cloud (r2 as ibm_phoenix ). Superconducting chips in dilution refrigerators, paired with laptop-to-supercomputer classical compute. Performance: r2 executes 100,000+ circuits per second, about 25x Heron, with Heron-class gate fidelity. Best: Up to 19x speedup over earlier IBM processors on partner workloads; E.ON reports 15x. Worst: r3 is a design, not shipping hardware. Chip-to-chip links average 99% state transfer fidelity, short of the 99.9% target. Bottom line: Best: real throughput gains on a cloud chip you can use now. Worst: the 1,040-qubit system is a 2027 plan, not a result. What is IBM Quantum Nighthawk? Nighthawk is IBM’s square-lattice processor family built for quantum advantage workloads. Most qubits connect to 4 nearest neighbors, versus 2 or 3 on earlier designs. That connectivity lets circuits express more entangling structure with fewer swap operations. The current production chip is Nighthawk r2 . It has 120 programmable qubits, 218 couplers and 120 reset elements. That is 458 physical quantum elements in total. How does Nighthawk r2 get 25x more throughput? The bottleneck was qubit reset. Heron uses conditional reset: measure, then flip any qubit found in the excited state. That method cannot fix leaked qubits, so the chip idles for hundreds of microseconds between shots. Nighthawk r2 replaces this with a dissipative reset gadget per qubit. A tunable coupler links each qubit to a cold environment on demand. This drops effective T1 from about 200 microseconds to roughly 25 nanoseconds. Idle time between runs falls to as little as 1 microsecond. The result is 100,000+ circuits per second. Heron manages roughly 4,000. IBM also reports about 25x lower initialization error, while neighbors stay undisturbed. What speedups are partners reporting? According to IBM, clients have run

summary.tldr:
IBM has announced IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3, a next-generation superconducting quantum processor designed to execute 10,000 accurate quantum operations across 520 programmable qubits. The company plans to link two r3 chips into a single 1,040-qubit system by 2027. Meanwhile, the current production chip, Nighthawk r2 (available on the IBM Quantum Platform cloud as ibm_phoenix), features 120 programmable qubits, 218 couplers, 120 reset elements, and a total of 2,034 physical qubits across the architecture. Nighthawk is a square-lattice processor family where most qubits connect to four nearest neighbors, reducing swap operations compared to earlier designs.

Nighthawk r2 achieves high throughput by replacing Heron's conditional reset method with a dissipative reset gadget per qubit, using a tunable coupler to link each qubit to a cold environment on demand. This drops effective T1 relaxation time from approximately 200 microseconds to roughly 25 nanoseconds, reducing idle time between runs to as little as 1 microsecond. Consequently, r2 executes over 100,000 circuits per second (about 25 times the throughput of Heron, which manages roughly 4,000), alongside 25x lower initialization error. Partner workloads show up to a 19x speedup over earlier IBM processors, with E.ON reporting a 15x speedup.

Despite the performance gains of the live r2 hardware, limitations remain. Nighthawk r3 is currently a design rather than shipping hardware, and the planned 1,040-qubit system is a 2027 roadmap target. Furthermore, chip-to-chip links currently average 99% state transfer fidelity, falling short of the required 99.9% target.
takeaways: **Nighthawk r3 Specifications:** Features 520 programmable qubits, 2,034 physical qubits, and 10 l-couplers, designed for 10,000 accurate quantum operations with a 1,040-qubit linked system targeted for 2027.
**Nighthawk r2 Specifications:** Features 120 programmable qubits, 218 couplers, 120 reset elements, and executes over 100,000 circuits per second with Heron-class gate fidelity.
**Dissipative Reset Innovation:** Drops effective T1 time from ~200 microseconds to ~25 nanoseconds and idle time between runs to 1 microsecond, yielding 25x higher throughput than Heron.
**Partner Performance:** Delivers up to 19x speedups over earlier IBM processors on partner workloads, including a 15x speedup reported by E.ON.
**Architectural Limitations:** Chip-to-chip links currently achieve 99% state transfer fidelity, which is below the 99.9% target, and r3 remains a design specification rather than shipping hardware.

title: Google’s GKE Labs turns reinforcement learning into a Kubernetes workload
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 20:51 EST / NOVEMBER 11 2026

Google’s GKE Labs turns reinforcement learning into a Kubernetes workload

Model fine-tuning through reinforcement learning is fast becoming one of the most demanding jobs in AI infrastructure. It mixes training, inference and sandboxed agent work in a single loop, often with research code tangled into the systems beneath it.

Google LLC has been tackling that problem from inside its Kubernetes engineering group, and recently donated the result, OpenRL, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation . The GKE Labs team got there by building an AI agent for Kubernetes tasks, then a benchmark to grade models on that work, according to Sunil Arora (pictured, left), senior software engineer at Google Cloud.

“If you look at reinforcement learning, I think of it as a kind of a super app of AI because it involves training. It involves sampling. It involves agents actually doing things in a sandbox and sometimes kind of evaluating the work,” Arora said. “It’s kind of a very diverse workload and it is, I think, pushing the boundaries of our infrastructure.”

Arora and Justin Santa Barbara (right), developer at Google, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed model fine-tuning and their work in GKE Labs, which puts experimental projects in users’ hands early. (* Disclosure below.)

Model fine-tuning without the infrastructure tangle

OpenRL debuted as a research preview in June 2026 , offering a self-hosted training API for a company’s own Kubernetes cluster. It splits the reinforcement learning loop from the compute plumbing, so infrastructure engineers handle scaling while researchers keep control of experiments, Arora explained.

“With OpenRL, one of the things that we are trying to do is kind of abstracting away the infrastructure as kind of core primitives so that researchers and AI engineers can just focus on their RL loop,” Arora said.

Sandboxes are where that loop meets agent infrastructure, since calculating rewards can mean running millions of isolated commands. Google’s Agent Substrate packs more of those sandboxes onto limited compute, according to Arora. For Santa Barbara, the need surfaced one step at a time.

“We built kubectl-ai, and in theory, kubectl-ai could have f

summary.tldr:
Google’s GKE Labs has introduced OpenRL, a framework designed to treat reinforcement learning (RL) model fine-tuning as a native Kubernetes workload. Donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), OpenRL aims to decouple the complex RL training loop—which involves simultaneous training, sampling, and agent evaluation—from the underlying compute infrastructure. By abstracting infrastructure into core primitives, the project allows researchers to focus on RL loops while infrastructure engineers manage scaling and resource allocation.

The architecture relies on Google’s 'Agent Substrate' to manage high-density sandboxing, which is critical for executing the millions of isolated commands required for reward calculation in RL. The project originated from internal GKE Labs experiments, including the development of 'kubectl-ai,' an AI agent for Kubernetes management. To mitigate security risks associated with autonomous agents—such as accidental disk formatting—the team implemented sandboxing to isolate agent actions from host systems. OpenRL was released as a research preview in June 2026 and provides a self-hosted training API for Kubernetes clusters.
takeaways: **Project Origin:** OpenRL was developed by Google’s GKE Labs and subsequently donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF).
**Core Functionality:** The framework provides a self-hosted training API that separates the RL training loop from compute plumbing to simplify infrastructure management.
**Security Architecture:** The system utilizes 'Agent Substrate' to pack isolated sandboxes onto limited compute, preventing autonomous agents (like kubectl-ai) from damaging host environments.
**Release Timeline:** OpenRL was first made available as a research preview in June 2026.

title: Google enters decision model market with Gemini Decisions API
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 20:22 EST / NOVEMBER 11 2026

Google enters decision model market with Gemini Decisions API

Google LLC today launched Gemini Decisions API, an artificial intelligence service designed to answer user questions in a cost-efficient manner.

It’s powered by a new AI model called Gemini Decision 1.

Traditional large language models are designed to answer a broad range of prompts. Gemini Decision 1 has a much narrower focus: It can process just three types of questions. The upside is that it answers those questions at a significantly lower cost. According to Google, the model is nearly five times cheaper than its entry-level Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite LLM.

The model can answer yes-no questions, multiple choice questions and prompts that ask it to rate an item on a user-specified scale. A cybersecurity team, for example, could ask the model to rate the severity of an antivirus alert on a scale of 1 to 10.

Gemini Decision 1 prompts include two items: the user’s questions and the dataset to which those questions pertain. The dataset can include up to 256,000 tokens worth of text, audio, images, video or some combination thereof.

LLMs usually generate verbose free-flowing text in response to user questions. Gemini Decision 1, in contrast, outputs terse answers such as “yes” or “no.” It also displays a score that indicates how confident it is in the accuracy of a given response. That score helps applications decide whether they should make use of the output.

Neural networks designed to generate brief answers to simple questions are known as decision models. The first such model, Jev, was launched in mid-September by a startup called TypeSafe AI Inc. It gained a million users within a few days. Three weeks after the launch, TypeSafe raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation.

Decision models can answer the narrow set of questions for which they’re optimized faster than LLMs. Additionally, they’re easier to integrate into applications. An application that powers some of its features using an AI model must check the model’s output for errors and filter redundant details before ingesting it. Decision models’ concise, structured responses make both tasks simpler.

“Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens,

summary.tldr:
Google has launched the Gemini Decisions API, powered by a specialized model called Gemini Decision 1. Unlike traditional large language models (LLMs) designed for open-ended text generation, this model is purpose-built for three specific tasks: yes-no questions, multiple-choice queries, and rating items on a user-defined scale. By narrowing the scope, Google claims the model is approximately five times cheaper than its Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite LLM, with pricing set at $0.10 per 1 million input tokens and no charge for output tokens.

Technically, Gemini Decision 1 processes multimodal datasets—including text, audio, images, and video—up to 256,000 tokens. The model avoids token-by-token decoding, achieving a median model compute latency of 50-100 ms (150-250 ms end-to-end) for contexts up to 16K tokens. It outputs concise, structured responses alongside a confidence score to assist in automated decision-making. Google reports that the model outperformed competitors, including TypeSafe AI’s 'Jev' and OpenAI’s 'Decisions API,' in seven out of nine internal benchmarks, though Jev remains slightly more cost-efficient.
takeaways: **Pricing Model:** Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1 million input tokens with zero cost for output tokens.
**Performance Metrics:** The model maintains a median end-to-end latency of 150-250 ms for contexts up to 16K tokens, with performance remaining stable for up to 100 questions per request.
**Input Capacity:** The API supports multimodal datasets (text, audio, images, video) up to a 256,000-token limit.
**Competitive Landscape:** Google claims Gemini Decision 1 outperformed OpenAI’s Decisions API and TypeSafe AI’s Jev in seven of nine internal benchmarks.
**Availability:** The service is currently accessible via the Gemini Decisions API and a limited free tier within Google AI Studio.

title: Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI

Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI close those gaps, so Java teams can build autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and APIs, and maintain context across multi-turn conversations. Agentic AI is moving beyond prompt-response interactions toward autonomous systems that execute complex multi-step tasks. It is framework-agnostic and model-agnostic: you bring your preferred agent framework and foundation model (FM). With AgentCore, you can access the production infrastructure you need: managed runtime, memory, browser automation, code execution, and identity management. In this post, we show you how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock with spring-ai-agentcore . We explore the key implementation patterns for two systems. summary.tldr:
Amazon and the Spring AI team have introduced a framework integration designed to bridge the gap between Java enterprise infrastructure and autonomous AI agent development. By utilizing Spring AI 2.0 and the newly introduced spring-ai-agentcore 2.0, Java developers can now leverage familiar idioms—such as dependency injection, auto-configuration, and composable advisors—to build agents capable of tool calling, multi-turn context management, and complex task execution. The integration aims to address common production hurdles like scalability, governance, and security that often plague prototype-to-production transitions in AI.

At the core of this architecture is Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a framework-agnostic and model-agnostic platform that provides managed runtime environments for AI agents. AgentCore supplies the necessary infrastructure for production-grade deployments, including identity management, memory, browser automation, and code execution. **AgentCore Capabilities:** Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides managed runtime, memory, browser automation, code execution, and identity management for agents.

title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
author: Amanda Silberling
contentSnippet:
Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security.

United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, the Times has reported.

The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.

Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang , and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.

As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang

After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per the Wa

summary.tldr:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing a mounting corporate and national security crisis following reports of an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based Megaspeed executive whom U.S. officials allege is a Chinese intelligence operative. The situation has escalated into a federal investigation by the Department of Justice, with House committee chairs threatening subpoenas if the CEO does not participate in a closed-door briefing regarding potential breaches of U.S. chip export restrictions. The controversy has triggered an internal board-led investigation and reports that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang, causing the company's stock to decline 11% over a five-day period.

Technical and commercial scrutiny centers on Megaspeed, an AI infrastructure firm that purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia hardware over two years. Investigations by U.S. and Singaporean authorities suggest Megaspeed acted as a conduit for bypassing export controls, with reports indicating the firm facilitated $7.5 billion in chip acquisitions, including restricted models, for Chinese entities like Alibaba. Further complicating the leadership crisis, the New York Times reported a second extramarital relationship between Jensen Huang and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s Vice President of Healthcare, who reports directly to him. Huang has admitted to infidelity in a public letter but has not confirmed specific details regarding the allegations involving Alice Huang.
takeaways: **Corporate Governance:** Nvidia’s board has initiated an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang, with reports suggesting active preparations for his removal following the dual-affair allegations.

**Export Control Violations:** Megaspeed International is under federal investigation for allegedly smuggling restricted Nvidia chips into China, with reports citing $7.5 billion in total chip acquisitions facilitated by the firm.

**Congressional Oversight:** Three House committee chairs—John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford—have requested a closed-door briefing, threatening a subpoena if Huang fails to address national security concerns.
**Market Impact:** Nvidia shares fell 8% in after-hours trading on November 11, 2026, contributing to an 11% decline over the preceding five-day period.

**Intelligence Allegations:** A secret memo supervised by Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly identified Alice Huang as an operative for China’s Ministry of State Security, a finding briefed to President Trump.

title: OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock
