title: Google DeepMind releases new advanced robotics AI model and next-generation gene prediction model
author: Kyt Dotson
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 11:30 EST / NOVEMBER 11 2026

Google DeepMind releases new advanced robotics AI model and next-generation gene prediction model

Alphabet Inc.’s artificial intelligence research lab, Google DeepMind, Tuesday debuted the next generation of Gemini Robotics , the company’s most capable vision-language-action model to date for creating an “AI brain” for robotics.

Separately, DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2 today, a next-generation AI model that can predict how DNA sequences and their variations affect human cell types, creating a powerful biological tool for fighting disease and drug development.

DeepMind said Gemini Robotics 2.5 enhances dexterity, reliability and safety to help engineers bring robots out of the lab and into dynamic, unstructured, real-world environments where they can coordinate alongside humans.

The company said that with the release of Gemini 4 Argon , the research division has been able to accelerate robot research and reach into physical AI. The new robotics AI model was tested across over 200 distinct tasks and the company said it anticipates scaling even further.

Argon, the company’s frontier artificial intelligence large language model, rolled out in late September, bringing advanced reasoning to the enterprise. Using the capabilities behind this new, flagship model, DeepMind said it allowed Gemini Robotics 2.5 to increase the breadth and speed with which robots can learn new skills and apply them to real-world scenarios.

The 2.5 version makes a significant jump in optimization and performance across three key areas. Boosted dexterity means robots running on 2.5 can perform more tasks with greater accuracy, including using everyday tools to handle delicate, flexible objects. With increased reliability, the new model successfully packed automotive parts with a 96% success rate during real-world proof-of-concept tests at Mercedes-Benz. Finally, DeepMind enhanced safety with improved physical steerability and introduced a new benchmark for testing against jailbreaks.

In evaluations, Robotics 2.5 now achieves a 30% to 100% success rate depending on the task and completes tasks 20% to 30% faster compared with the previous version’s baseline.

The company said that, like previous models, it natively works with many different types of robots, including Apptronik Inc.’s Apollo 2 humanoid robots and the Franka Duo platform with tw

summary.tldr:
Alphabet Inc.’s Google DeepMind debuted two next-generation models on November 11, 2026: Gemini Robotics 2.5, a vision-language-action model functioning as an AI brain for robots, and AlphaGenome 2, a biological tool predicting how DNA sequences and variations affect specific human cell types. Gemini Robotics 2.5 integrates capabilities from DeepMind's flagship Gemini 4 Argon large language model—released in late September—to accelerate skill acquisition and physical AI research.

Tested across more than 200 distinct tasks, Gemini Robotics 2.5 achieves a 30% to 100% success rate depending on the task and executes actions 20% to 30% faster than its predecessor. Real-world proof-of-concept tests at Mercedes-Benz demonstrated a 96% success rate in packing automotive parts. The model natively supports multiple robot hardware platforms including Apptronik Inc.'s Apollo 2 humanoid robots and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered parallel grippers, and is rolling out via partners such as Agile Robots SE and Boston Dynamics Inc.

AlphaGenome 2 incorporates data from the Human Cell Atlas consortium to predict single-cell gene expression, histone modification, chromatin accessibility, and newly added DNA methylation for epigenetics. According to University of Cambridge Professor Sarah Teichmann, the model adapts directly to new single-cell data from small samples without retraining. DeepMind notes that AlphaGenome 2 guides research rather than replacing experimental validation and is not approved for clinical or diagnostic use.
takeaways: **Gemini Robotics 2.5 Performance:** Achieves a 30% to 100% success rate across more than 200 tested tasks and completes tasks 20% to 30% faster than baseline models.
**Mercedes-Benz Proof of Concept:** Achieved a 96% success rate packing automotive parts during real-world trials.
**Hardware Integration:** Natively supports platforms including Apptronik Apollo 2 humanoids and the Franka Duo platform, deploying via partners Agile Robots SE, Apptronik, and Boston Dynamics.

**AlphaGenome 2 Capabilities:** Predicts gene expression, histone modification, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation across specific human cell types without requiring retraining on new single-cell data.

title: AI agents carry memory and storage like people, so their data needs guarding while in use
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 11:20 EST / NOVEMBER 11 2026

AI agents carry memory and storage like people, so their data needs guarding while in use

As AI agents move into production on Kubernetes, cloud engineering teams at financial companies face a security problem that encryption alone can’t solve. Container orchestration has become the default foundation for AI workloads, and the data those agents use is now the main target.

Payment networks feel that pressure more than most because every transaction carries customer data and regulatory exposure. Protecting data while it is being processed, and not just while it is stored or moving, has become central to running agents at scale, according to Krishna Mayuram (pictured), senior principal engineer and vice president of cloud engineering at Mastercard Inc.

“What we call confidential computing is when you are launching these applications in a highly secure, virtualized secure environments or confidential environments or confidential containers, you are able to protect the data in use,” Mayuram said. “We have protected data at rest, data in motion. Now, what is happening to the data in use?”

Mayuram spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed cloud engineering, security problems and the challenges of protecting data in use. (* Disclosure below.)

Cloud engineering for agents runs on guardrails

Mastercard runs its platforms on Red Hat Inc.’s OpenShift, a Kubernetes platform that Red Hat is extending to support AI agents. Red Hat has also brought confidential containers to OpenShift on bare metal. Agents act much like microservices and need the same elastic infrastructure, Mayuram explained.

“We need to scale the platform, that’s Kubernetes which gives horizontal scaling, vertical scaling, if you will, and also the agents, just like applications, require all the elastic capabilities of Kubernetes,” Mayuram said.

Scale increases the risk, especially for a company that operates under many countries’ laws. Mastercard recently added trust services for agentic commerce. Internally, the same idea applies, with guardrails at every step from development to deployment, according to Mayuram.

“The business is distributed, the industry is very distributed, and we have different laws of t

summary.tldr:
At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, Mastercard’s Senior Principal Engineer and VP of Cloud Engineering, Krishna Mayuram, highlighted the critical security gap in deploying AI agents within Kubernetes environments: protecting data while it is in use. As AI agents function similarly to microservices, they require the same elastic infrastructure for horizontal and vertical scaling, but their memory and storage usage patterns introduce new vulnerabilities that traditional encryption at rest or in transit cannot mitigate. Mastercard is addressing these risks by implementing confidential computing, which utilizes secure, virtualized environments to isolate and protect data during active processing.

Mastercard leverages Red Hat OpenShift as its primary Kubernetes platform, which is currently being extended to support agentic workloads. The company is utilizing Red Hat’s confidential containers on bare metal to enforce security guardrails throughout the development and deployment lifecycle. These guardrails are designed to maintain enterprise-grade security standards while navigating the complex regulatory requirements of a distributed, global financial business. The strategy emphasizes that regardless of whether a workload is a standard application or an AI agent, the underlying security requirements for data protection remain consistent.
takeaways: **Confidential Computing Focus:** Mastercard is prioritizing the protection of 'data in use' via confidential containers to secure AI agent memory and storage during active processing.
**Infrastructure Foundation:** Mastercard utilizes Red Hat OpenShift on bare metal as the Kubernetes-based platform for scaling AI agents.
**Agentic Security Strategy:** The company applies uniform enterprise security guardrails to AI agents, treating them as microservices that require elastic scaling capabilities.
**Regulatory Compliance:** The security architecture is designed to accommodate diverse international laws governing financial transactions and customer data.

title: Is Jensen Huang’s bad behavior more commonplace than it seems?
author: Russell Brandom
contentSnippet:
The AI industry is still reeling from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s honeypot scandal, but some in the industry see it as an issue that’s much larger than one man.

The Chinese government has been active in economic espionage for decades, and with semiconductors at the center of the AI boom, there’s intense pressure to infiltrate any company involved. At the same time, many of the executives getting rich off that boom have made themselves easy targets.

As CEO of investment intel firm Heron Intelligence, Nate Singer has a unique view into the problem. His firm works on corporate due diligence: Essentially, making sure companies know the relevant dirt before making a major acquisition or executive hire. And while the Nvidia case is particularly severe, Singer says there are lots of similar cases in the semiconductor industry that have stayed under the radar.

“We’ve got former employees talking about behavior at senior executive levels,” Singer told TechCrunch, saying executives are “really crossing lines that should not be crossed.”

In a widely circulated LinkedIn post , Singer detailed one case in which a CEO’s wife made an unexpected board room appearance, “screaming about her husband and another company exec flying around in the corporate jet with a couple young ladies (who also turned out to be state-sponsored actors).”

It’s an alarming story, but an unfortunately common one. Singer says he’s seen at least three reports of similar cases, and suspects many more have gone unreported.

“There’s a lot more than this one woman,” Singer said. “They are embedded in these companies.”

Semiconductor companies are already big targets for international trade secret theft. There have been dozens of prosecutions for similar cases in recent years, including a case involving the fabrication powerhouse TSMC in 2006.

In 2017, four executives at an unnamed “Bay Area semiconductor equipment manufacturer” were charged with stealing trade secrets for use at a competing company in China. According to the indictment, the technology in question “related to the high-volume manufacturing of semiconductor wafers to be used in lighting and electronic devices, such as flat screen televisions and smart phones.“

Any sexual elements in such cases rarely become public, in part because of the severe consequences for executives and their companies. But according to Singer, the ongoing thre

summary.tldr:
Nate Singer, CEO of corporate due diligence firm Heron Intelligence, reports that the semiconductor industry faces a systemic issue regarding executive vulnerability to state-sponsored espionage. Singer suggests that the recent controversy involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is part of a broader, often unreported pattern where senior executives are targeted by foreign intelligence actors using honeypot tactics. These incidents frequently involve the compromise of corporate leadership through personal indiscretions that are then leveraged to gain access to sensitive trade secrets.

According to Singer, these security breaches are an 'open secret' among industry leadership, with many cases remaining private to avoid the severe reputational and legal consequences associated with such scandals. He cites specific instances, including a documented case where a CEO's spouse confronted board members regarding the CEO’s use of a corporate jet to transport state-sponsored actors. These activities mirror historical patterns of industrial espionage, such as the 2006 TSMC case and the 2017 indictment of four executives at a Bay Area semiconductor equipment manufacturer for stealing wafer manufacturing trade secrets for Chinese competitors.
takeaways: **Heron Intelligence Findings:** CEO Nate Singer reports having seen at least three documented cases of executives being targeted by state-sponsored actors via honeypot schemes in the semiconductor sector.

**Historical Precedent:** The semiconductor industry has a long history of trade secret theft, including the 2006 TSMC case and a 2017 indictment involving the theft of high-volume semiconductor wafer manufacturing technology.

**Industry Complicity:** Singer alleges that many senior industry figures are aware of these security compromises and are effectively condoning the behavior by failing to address the underlying vulnerabilities.

**Espionage Tactics:** State-sponsored actors are reportedly embedding themselves within companies by exploiting the personal behavior of high-level executives to gain access to proprietary manufacturing and trade data.

title: OpenAI’s quarterly revenue reportedly crosses $10B for the first time
author: Ram Iyer
contentSnippet: Sales of $10 billion represents an almost 50% jump from revenue of $6.7 billion the company recorded in the second quarter.

summary.tldr:
OpenAI has reportedly surpassed $10 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time, marking a nearly 50% increase from the $6.7 billion recorded in the second quarter. This growth represents a significant acceleration compared to the 18% quarter-over-quarter growth observed between Q1 and Q2. The company’s adjusted operating margin also showed improvement, narrowing from -150% in the second quarter to -109% in the third quarter, according to Bloomberg.

Despite this growth, OpenAI faces intense competition from Anthropic, which reported $17 billion in Q3 revenue and an annual revenue run rate of $81 billion as of late October. OpenAI currently maintains an annual revenue run rate of $50 billion. These figures are subject to different accounting methodologies: Anthropic includes sales generated through cloud partners, whereas OpenAI reports only its specific share of partner-facilitated sales. OpenAI’s recent performance is attributed to a strategic shift toward enterprise-focused products, AI agents, and refined pricing models, even as it contends with competition from major tech incumbents like Meta, Google, Microsoft, and Amazon.
takeaways: **Quarterly Revenue Growth:** OpenAI reached $10 billion in Q3 revenue, a ~50% increase over the $6.7 billion reported in Q2.
**Operating Margin:** OpenAI's adjusted operating margin improved from -150% in Q2 to -109% in Q3.
**Annual Run Rate Comparison:** OpenAI reports a $50 billion annual revenue run rate, while Anthropic reports an $81 billion run rate as of October.
**Accounting Discrepancy:** Anthropic includes total sales from cloud partners in its revenue figures, while OpenAI counts only its specific share of those sales.

title: Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick
author: Vishnu Elangovan
contentSnippet: This blog post focuses on how AI can improve and expedite the product development life cycle using agents built on AWS Quick, with human approval baked into the process. AI-driven software delivery is helping teams ship products faster than ever. As implementation accelerates, the upstream product development process becomes even more important. Coding agents can turn clear requirements into working software faster than before, but they can’t compensate for building the wrong product. With implementation becoming easier, your competitive advantage moves upstream to four critical activities: discovering the right customer problem, deciding which opportunity to pursue, designing the right experience, and validating it through a prototype. The signals that you need to make those decisions are scattered everywhere. Your customers leave feedback in Slack, your sales team logs insights in Salesforce, systems record incidents in ServiceNow, stakeholders document requirements in Microsoft SharePoint, engineers track work items in Jira, and teams make decisions in Outlook meetings and email threads. As your teams move between these tools, they disconnect context from the decisions it should inform, and lose more at every handoff. AWS Quick provides the connective layer for this fragmented knowledge. By grounding custom chat agents in connected enterprise data and storing their artifacts in shared Spaces , AWS Quick helps your team build with existing organizational knowledge instead of starting each initiative from a blank page. The AI-Driven Product Development Lifecycle (AI-PDLC) is a framework that applies these capabilities through a suite of six AWS Quick agents with specialized skills, producing a traceable set of artifacts at each phase. Agents gather and structure context, surface gaps, and draft artifacts. You and your team contribute judgment and approve every decision. The objective isn’t to produce documents faster. It’s to help your team think better, preserve why each decision was made, and give engineering and coding agents a specification grounded in customer evidence. We will show you how to configure the six-agent AI-PDLC suite in AWS Quick and use it to move from distributed customer signals to a validated prototype. Throughout, it preserves context from the first insight through the engineering handoff. Architecture The diagram shows the end-to-en

summary.tldr:
AWS has introduced the AI-Driven Product Development Lifecycle (AI-PDLC), a framework designed to integrate fragmented enterprise data into a unified workflow using AWS Quick. The system aims to address the bottleneck of upstream product development—specifically discovery, opportunity assessment, design, and prototyping—by grounding custom AI agents in data sourced from tools including Slack, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Microsoft SharePoint, Jira, Outlook, and email. By centralizing this information in AWS Quick 'Spaces,' the framework seeks to prevent context loss during handoffs and ensure that downstream coding agents receive specifications backed by documented customer evidence.

The AI-PDLC framework utilizes a suite of six specialized AWS Quick agents. These agents are tasked with gathering and structuring context, identifying information gaps, and drafting development artifacts. The architecture emphasizes a 'human-in-the-loop' model, where the AI generates drafts and surfaces insights, but human teams retain final approval authority for every decision. The primary objective is to maintain a traceable audit trail of why specific product decisions were made, moving beyond simple document generation to improve the quality of the product specification process before engineering begins.
takeaways: **Data Integration:** The framework aggregates signals from Slack, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Microsoft SharePoint, Jira, and Outlook to ground AI agents in organizational knowledge.
**Agent Architecture:** The AI-PDLC suite consists of six specialized agents that manage the product development lifecycle from initial customer insight to engineering handoff.
**Human Oversight:** The system mandates human approval for all AI-generated artifacts to ensure decision-making remains under team control.

**Core Objective:** The framework focuses on preserving decision context and evidence-based specifications to prevent the common issue of building the wrong product despite faster coding capabilities.

title: Google’s Tabletop AI experiment lets you build custom collaboration apps
author: Jess Weatherbed
contentSnippet: Google has cooked up a new experimental AI tool called Tabletop that generates customized collaborative hubs to help you coordinate with family, and friends. The Tabletop platform shares some visual similarities with workplace management apps like Asana and Monday, but with a built-in AI feature that allows you to vibecode personalized interactive tools by describing them, such as savings trackers, chore charts, event plans, and more. “Just add in your links, files and ideas, then prompt @tabletop — or pick a starter template — to generate custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets,” Google Labs design and engineering lead Roman Nurik said in the blog post. “Once your space is ready, drop the invite link in your group chat to let everyone jump in and use it at the same time like a Google Doc.” [Video: Google Labs Tabletop AI] Access to the Tabletop beta is rolling out via a waitlist, and currently limited to people over the age of 18 in the US. Some of the example use cases that Nurik provides in his video above would clearly require giving kids or teens access to Tabletop, however, and using this for personal family planning looks like a compelling alternative to stuffy workplace software, so that age requirement might only be in place while Tabletop is in public testing.

summary.tldr:
Google Labs has introduced Tabletop, an experimental AI-powered platform designed to generate customized collaborative hubs for personal use. The tool allows users to create interactive applications—such as chore charts, expense splitters, event planners, and tournament brackets—by providing natural language prompts or selecting from pre-built starter templates. The interface functions similarly to project management software like Asana or Monday, but is specifically tailored for non-professional coordination among friends and family.

Users can populate these spaces with links, files, and ideas, which the AI then organizes into functional, real-time collaborative tools. Once generated, these hubs are shareable via invite links, enabling multiple users to interact with the content simultaneously, similar to the collaborative experience of a Google Doc. The platform is currently in a public beta phase, accessible via a waitlist for users aged 18 and older within the United States.
takeaways: **Core Functionality:** Users can generate custom interactive tools like savings trackers and dinner polls by prompting the @tabletop AI or using starter templates.
**Collaboration Model:** The platform supports real-time multi-user interaction via shareable links, mirroring the collaborative workflow of Google Docs.
**Target Audience:** The tool is positioned as a personal alternative to enterprise-grade project management software like Asana or Monday.
**Availability:** Access is currently restricted to a US-based waitlist for individuals 18 years of age or older.

title: Agents may soon be the main workload, and most of the time they’re doing nothing
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 10:59 EST / NOVEMBER 11 2026

Agents may soon be the main workload, and most of the time they’re doing nothing

As AI agents take on more enterprise work, agent sandboxing has become a basic requirement rather than an afterthought. Every agent that writes code, runs tools or drives a browser needs hard walls around it. Those walls also can’t come at the cost of runaway compute bills.

Google LLC’s answer is Agent Substrate, an open-source project built on Kubernetes that the company donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation alongside its gVisor sandbox. Customers have raised the same problem for the past 18 months: They need to run agentic workloads securely and efficiently on the infrastructure they already have, according to Brandon Royal (pictured, left), product manager, AI agents and infrastructure, at Google Cloud.

“Any agent needs to be fully isolated,” Royal said. “Whether it’s accessing tools or using a computer or a browser, there needs to be some level of isolation, period, full stop.”

Royal and Benjamin Elder (right), staff software engineer at Google, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how agent sandboxing is central to Google’s open-source Agent Substrate. (* Disclosure below.)

Agent sandboxing that locks down by default

Agent Substrate starts with hardened sandbox runtimes densely packed on Kubernetes clusters. All traffic passes through a layer that applies policy and understands identity, so an agent can reach nothing it hasn’t been explicitly granted, Elder explained. The project also keeps secrets out of the agent’s hands by injecting credentials on the wire.

“Don’t expose credentials to the sandbox,” Elder said. “Don’t let the agent touch the credentials. Instead, when it requests to do something, you can make a decision about outside the sandbox.”

Security is only half the equation. Agents in a swarm spend much of their time blocked, waiting on a large language model call or on a human to follow up. Agent Substrate snapshots those idle agents out of memory and CPU, stores them offline and restores them when they’re needed, freeing resources across the cluster, according to Elder.

“Should you be holding compute while you’re getting coffee? Because you might co

summary.tldr:
Google LLC has introduced Agent Substrate, an open-source project donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) designed to provide secure, efficient infrastructure for AI agent workloads. Built on Kubernetes and integrated with Google’s gVisor sandbox technology, the project addresses the dual challenges of agent isolation and resource optimization. According to Google product manager Brandon Royal and staff software engineer Benjamin Elder, the platform is intended to serve as a foundational layer for enterprise AI agents that require strict security boundaries when executing code, accessing tools, or interacting with browsers.

Technically, Agent Substrate utilizes hardened sandbox runtimes to enforce policy and identity-based access control. To prevent security vulnerabilities, the system avoids exposing credentials directly to the sandbox, instead injecting them on the wire only when necessary. To manage the high idle time inherent in agentic workflows—where agents often wait for LLM responses or human input—the platform employs a snapshotting mechanism. This feature moves idle agents out of active memory and CPU, storing them offline and restoring them only when required, thereby increasing cluster density and reducing compute costs. Google is already utilizing this architecture for its Gemini Managed Agents and the recently launched Agent Compute Engine.
takeaways: **Core Architecture:** Agent Substrate is an open-source project built on Kubernetes and gVisor, donated to the CNCF to standardize agent sandboxing.
**Credential Security:** The platform prevents credential exposure by keeping secrets out of the sandbox and injecting them only at the point of action.
**Resource Optimization:** The system includes a snapshotting feature that offloads idle agents from memory and CPU to improve cluster efficiency.
**Commercial Integration:** Google’s Gemini Managed Agents and Agent Compute Engine are currently built on the Agent Substrate framework.

title: Marktechpost AI Launches GPU Leaderboard and the Deploy It Chrome Extension
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Marktechpost has launched GPU Leaderboard , a free cloud GPU price comparison for AI inference. It also shipped GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It , a Chrome extension for the same data. The site reads on-demand and spot prices from each provider’s own pricing page. The goal is simple: answer “what GPU do I need, and where is it cheapest?” in one place. What is GPU Leaderboard? GPU Leaderboard is a pricing dashboard that ranks rentable cloud GPUs by price per GPU-hour. It is built for teams running inference. The v1 application has 4 views: Inference pricing: a cost calculator for a full run, not a single hourly rate. Leaderboard : every offer ranked by $/GPU-hr, filterable by GPU, tier, region and availability. Cheapest Inference : the lowest on-demand floor for each tracked GPU. Providers : a directory with instance counts, regions, status-page incidents and price-check history. How does the GPU inference cost calculator work? You pick an accelerator, GPU count, duration and utilization. The calculator then prices that exact run at every provider. An optional model field narrows the list. The default example is 8×H100 for 72 hours at 90% utilization. That bills 576 GPU-hours. The cheapest result is $967.68 at Latitude, at $1.68 per GPU-hour. The median across 15 providers is $1,716.48. The most expensive is $3,545.28 at CoreWeave. The calculator also shows a “real” cost per used GPU-hour. Idle time is still billed, so $1.68 at 90% utilization becomes $1.87. The tool aggregates real-time on-demand and spot pricing directly from provider websites, allowing users to rank rentable cloud GPUs by price per GPU-hour. Alongside the web dashboard, the company released a Chrome extension titled 'GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It' to provide integrated access to this pricing data.

The platform features four primary views: an inference cost calculator, a ranked leaderboard, a 'Cheapest Inference' floor tracker, and a provider directory. The cost calculator accounts for GPU count, duration, and utilization rates to estimate total run costs. For example, a 72-hour run using 8x H100 GPUs at 90% utilization results in a cost range from $967.68 at Latitude ($1.68/GPU-hr) to $3,545.28 at CoreWeave, with a median cost of $1,716.48 across 15 providers. The tool also calculates 'real' cost per used GPU-hour by factoring in idle time billing, which is often omitted in standard budget projections.
takeaways: **Platform Scope:** Tracks 15 cloud GPU providers with data on instance counts, regional availability, and historical price checks.
**Calculator Methodology:** Estimates total run costs by incorporating utilization percentages, which adjusts the effective hourly rate to account for idle time billing.
**Benchmark Example:** An 8x H100 configuration for 72 hours at 90% utilization shows a price variance of approximately 3.6x between the cheapest ($967.68) and most expensive ($3,545.28) providers.
**Tooling:** Offers both a web-based dashboard and a Chrome extension for real-time price discovery during the deployment workflow.

title: UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents
author: Samaneh Aminikhanghahi
contentSnippet: Teams building AI agents on AWS use a range of frameworks, including LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each framework records agent execution in its own way, so the structure of messages, tool calls, and handoffs between agents differs from one to the next. Evaluation tooling tends to follow the same boundaries: teams build metrics, scoring logic, and result storage against a single framework’s trace format, and they must rebuild them when they switch frameworks or run agents on more than one. This coupling makes a basic development question harder to answer: did a change to the prompt, model, or tools improve the agent? Answering it requires consistent metrics across versions of an agent and a shared record of past results to compare against. Agent quality also spans several dimensions that a single accuracy score does not capture: tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi-turn conversation, multi-agent coordination, and reasoning. In this post, we introduce the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF). Customers across 12 organizations in the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries used UAEF to evaluate their AI agents with one consistent set of metrics and compare agent versions before release. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system: it uses adapters to convert traces from each framework into a common format, then scores those traces with 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions. It stores the results in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and generates reports and insights that inform the next iteration of the agent. This post describes how UAEF works, provides a playbook for choosing metrics and preparing datasets, and points to runnable notebooks for each supported framework. UAEF: One evaluation layer for agent frameworks UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system for AI agents. It takes the agent a team already has and scores it the same way across supported frameworks and runtimes. UAEF takes two inputs: the agent under test and a dataset to run it on. The dataset provides the inputs for each test case, and it can also include ground-truth answers, the expected output for each input. Ground truth is optional, and only metrics that compare the agent’s response against a reference use it. To evaluate tool calling, the ground truth must als

summary.tldr:
Amazon has introduced the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF), a framework-agnostic system designed to standardize the evaluation of AI agents across diverse development environments. Currently, teams building on AWS utilize disparate frameworks such as LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, each with unique trace formats that complicate cross-framework performance comparisons. UAEF addresses this fragmentation by utilizing adapters to normalize execution traces into a common format, enabling consistent metric application regardless of the underlying agent architecture.

The system evaluates agents across 36 built-in metrics spanning seven core dimensions: tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi-turn conversation, multi-agent coordination, and reasoning. UAEF operates by ingesting an agent and a test dataset—which may optionally include ground-truth references—and storing the resulting evaluation data in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3). The framework has been validated through deployments across 12 organizations within the telecom, healthcare, and financial services sectors, providing a unified layer for tracking agent improvements across prompt, model, or tool iterations.
takeaways: **Supported Frameworks:** UAEF currently supports LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
**Evaluation Metrics:** The system includes 36 built-in metrics categorized into 7 distinct dimensions of agent quality.
**Data Infrastructure:** Evaluation results are persisted using Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3 for reporting and longitudinal comparison.
**Deployment Scope:** The framework has been tested by 12 organizations across the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries.

title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's mult

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has initiated its IPO roadshow, revealing a strategic focus on a hardware-agnostic infrastructure approach. Co-founder Tom Brown detailed the company's multi-chip strategy, which involves training and serving the Claude model family across four distinct hardware architectures: AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. This approach deviates from industry norms that typically favor single-vendor stacks, requiring Anthropic to develop and maintain custom software and inference stacks for each platform.

A key technical milestone highlighted in the roadshow is the integration of AMD GPUs, which was accelerated by an internal tool named Mythos. According to Brown, Mythos enabled the porting of Claude to AMD hardware in three days with minimal human intervention, with the tool reportedly writing or porting nearly 100% of the necessary kernels. This capability is presented as a core component of Anthropic's "compute advantage," which the company defines as the product of physical capacity and "compute multipliers."

Anthropic defines compute multipliers as efficiency gains that reduce the physical compute required to train a model of a specific intelligence level. The company claims these multipliers are cumulative and stackable, creating a compounding competitive advantage. Looking forward, Anthropic anticipates that future iterations of Claude will be capable of discovering these compute multipliers autonomously, potentially leading to a cycle of recursive self-improvement that accelerates the growth of their effective compute pool.
takeaways: **Hardware Diversity:** Anthropic currently trains and serves Claude across four major chip families: AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.
**Mythos Tooling:** The company utilized an internal tool called Mythos to port Claude to AMD GPUs in three days, with the tool handling nearly 100% of kernel generation.

**Compute Multiplier Strategy:** Anthropic defines its compute advantage as the product of physical capacity and "compute multipliers," which are efficiency gains that reduce the physical compute required for training.

**Recursive Improvement:** Anthropic projects that future versions of Claude will autonomously discover new compute multipliers, creating a compounding effect on their total effective compute capacity.

title: Introducing usage-based pricing for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming
author: Victor Wang
contentSnippet: Usage-based metering for bidirectional streaming solves a software billing problem for real-time speech AI. Customers deploying streaming models on Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming pay for the endpoint infrastructure that hosts the model. Separately, model providers listing on AWS Marketplace need a way to charge for what customers consume during a live stream. Today, we’re announcing usage-based metering for Amazon SageMaker bidirectional (bidi) streaming inference, so model providers can report actual usage for the AWS Marketplace software charge. Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges still apply. Deepgram , the real-time speech AI company, is the launch partner for this capability, bringing usage-based Speech-to-Text (STT) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) billing to AWS Marketplace. This post builds on a series of innovations between Deepgram and AWS. First, we introduced bidirectional streaming for real-time inference on Amazon SageMaker AI , which supports long-lived bidirectional streams between clients and model servers. Then, Deepgram enhanced Amazon SageMaker AI support with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) temporary delegation , simplifying secure authentication for enterprise deployments, and expanded observability with enhanced metrics . Now, with usage-based metering, we further strengthen the foundation for production real-time AI, aligning billing with how customers consume streaming and real-time AI workloads. Why streaming broke the existing billing model With AWS Marketplace software metering for SageMaker AI real-time request-response inference, model providers can report a unit count in an HTTP response header. AWS Marketplace uses that quantity for the software charge. This works for request-response APIs where the billable quantity is known when the response is sent. Bidirectional streaming is different. A client streams audio and receives transcriptions through the SageMaker AI API using an HTTP/2 event stream. SageMaker AI connects to the model server over WebSockets. A session can last 30 seconds or 30 minutes. Usage accumulates as the session runs, and the final total isn’t known until it ends. A response header alone can’t report periodic usage during that live session. Hourly software pricing can charge customers while a model is available, including quiet periods. With usage-based metering, providers

summary.tldr:
AWS has introduced usage-based metering for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional (bidi) streaming inference, enabling third-party model providers on AWS Marketplace to bill customers based on actual consumption during live streams. Previously, AWS Marketplace software metering relied on HTTP response headers, which are unsuitable for long-lived, asynchronous bidirectional streams where the final usage total is unknown until the session terminates. This update allows providers to report usage metrics periodically throughout a session rather than relying on fixed hourly charges that accrue even during periods of inactivity.

Deepgram is the launch partner for this capability, integrating it into their real-time Speech-to-Text (STT) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) offerings. This development follows previous collaborations between AWS and Deepgram, including the implementation of bidirectional streaming for real-time inference, AWS IAM temporary delegation for secure authentication, and enhanced observability metrics. While this new metering applies to the software charge for models listed on the AWS Marketplace, customers remain responsible for separate Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure costs.
takeaways: **Metering Mechanism:** Providers can now report usage metrics for bidirectional streaming sessions that persist over HTTP/2 event streams and WebSockets, overcoming the limitations of traditional request-response HTTP header billing.
**Launch Partner:** Deepgram is the first provider to utilize this capability for their STT and TTS models on the AWS Marketplace.
**Billing Structure:** The new system separates software usage charges from the underlying Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure costs, which continue to be billed independently.
**Technical Context:** The feature addresses the specific challenge of long-lived sessions (ranging from 30 seconds to 30+ minutes) where total consumption is not finalized until the stream closes.

title: AlphaGenome 2: Deciphering how cells read DNA to better understand disease
author: Google DeepMind
contentSnippet:
Adam Gayoso, Natasha Latysheva, Pushmeet Kohli and Žiga Avsec

Our next-generation DNA sequence model bridges single-cell biology and human genetics, predicting how genetic variants affect hundreds of human cell types.

Today, we are announcing AlphaGenome 2, our next-generation model that predicts how DNA sequences and their variations impact specific human cell types, giving scientists a powerful new tool to uncover the cellular drivers of disease.

Cells are the building blocks of life. Every cell in our body carries the same DNA blueprint, yet each cell type and state—like a heart muscle cell or an immune cell fighting an infection—switches different genes on or off to do its job. Global efforts like the Human Cell Atlas are mapping this gene expression for millions of cells, but it is still an unsolved challenge to predict how subtle DNA variations affect this expression in cells, which is a key driver of human traits and disease.

Last year, we launched AlphaGenome to predict how DNA variants affect molecular activity across broad tissues. We expanded its reach with AlphaGenome Atlas , a platform containing predictions for all 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome. These tools help researchers prioritize and interpret variant effects, driving discoveries in rare diseases, complex traits, and fundamental biology.

By zooming in from broad tissue averages to individual cell types and cell states, and redesigning the model’s architecture, AlphaGenome 2 represents a step-change improvement in variant predictive performance. Importantly, it allows researchers to predict variant effects in disease-relevant cells that would be missed in broad-tissue models, as well as predictions for cell and disease states that the model hasn’t seen before.

AlphaGenome 2 identifies nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression in cells, compared to our previous state-of-the-art model. Trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues, the model turns static cell atlases into a predictive engine for human genetics. AlphaGenome 2 is available today for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API, and in private preview for commercial research.

title: When Does It Actually Make Sense to Put AI Into Products?
author: Stephen Cousins
contentSnippet: Over the past few years, the tech industry has rushed to plug a new microchip into every device on the assumption that if you can add AI, you should. Smart-vision toothbrushes , mood-reading household robots , and a host of physical products are invading consumers’ daily lives, reliant on artificial intelligence to learn, predict, and adjust our behavior. But as anyone who’s struggled to update the firmware in their fridge knows, AI doesn’t improve every product. Some product designers are asking where the line is between genuine innovation and a solution looking for a problem. Savannah Kunovsky leads a team of industrial product designers at Ideo , a design consultancy based in San Francisco focused on helping clients unpack when AI becomes a barrier rather than a breakthrough. Kunovsky spoke with IEEE Spectrum about the pressure to integrate AI in everything, where that integration goes wrong, and what companies can do to determine when an AI integration is—and isn’t—a smart choice. When AI makes products worse How much of the current wave of AI integration into physical products is driven by pressure from investors and shareholders to keep up with industry trends? Savannah Kunovsky : Some of it. Teams come to us feeling pressured to show they’re doing something with AI, sometimes because a CEO has promised the board an “AI story” before the next earnings call, or a competitor has just launched an AI-powered version of their product. In all cases, the first thing we do is step back and ask who the product is for and what they’re trying to do. Once that’s clear, the role AI should play, whether large, small, or invisible, usually becomes obvious. There is an appetite for this kind of grounding in the industry right now. People want to cut through the hype and see what works in practice. How do you distinguish between a genuinely helpful AI feature and a gimmick? Kunovsky : The test for an AI gimmick is the same test we’d apply to any product experience: Does it help someone do what they’re trying to do? Answering that means understanding how people would use the product in the real context they’ll be using it. Many companies look straight to large language models (LLMs) because that’s top of their mind, but there is a whole AI toolbox to draw from: computer vision, sensor fusion, on-device models, et cetera. Picking the right capability for the task matters

title: NSF’s X-Labs Program Draws Support From Charities and Investors
author: Lucas Laursen
contentSnippet: When the U.S. National Science Foundation began its X-Labs program in May, the agency said the higher-risk, higher-funded awards would create new kinds of partnerships that would confront urgent scientific and technological challenges. Now the NSF is doubling down on the idea, with an announcement in October that charities, companies, and investment funds would provide X-Lab winners practical support such as laboratory space, software, shared equipment, and access to key data and expert guidance. The help provided by these organizations, which the NSF is calling “ consortium partners ,” will not give them ownership stakes in the X-Labs projects. The addition of the consortium partners may help the initial winners—who will be announced later in November or December and receive US $1.5 million for a 9-month planning phase—reach the aggressive targets needed to compete for much larger $50 million multiyear grants. “It’s a way of telling X-Labs applicants you don’t need to reinvent the wheel, so you’re not spending half of your X-Labs money to go build or buy basic infrastructure,” says Matt Cimaglia , an investor in consortium partners Occam Foundry and Florida Quantum Center . NSF X-Labs Focus on AI, Computing, and More The NSF initially announced two focus areas for the X-Labs program: scientific instruments for sensing and imaging and photonic microchips for quantum systems . In September, the agency followed up with three additional areas in AI for physical devices , decoding biological sequences , and pushing the physical limits of computing . The NSF requires potential X-Labs award recipients to eventually demonstrate autonomy : Leaders for projects must be focused on the work full-time, for example, and must be able to make hiring and spending decisions independently from any university or commercial owners. That agility sets X-Labs apart, along with the risk appetite. Consortium partners saw the potential to provide infrastructure and operations support to allow X-Labs recipients to focus on research. “[We’re] very interested in the enabling structures of R&D,” says Joshua M. Greenberg , program director at the Sloan Foundation, one of the participating partners. Greenberg says that the foundation has supported multiple focused research organizations, or FROs, already.
